title: The Apex Integration Architecture: Ten Programs as One System: Signature Edition
body:
The Signature edition of the apex integration architecture is a Signature original design, labeled Signature throughout, mirroring the public architecture component for component with Signature completions where the public design leaves a step open.

The starting combination named in the source paste, programs 1, 13, 21, 23, 27, 47, 52, 56, 78, and 100, is treated here as ONE integrated architecture, not as ten separate wishes. Each component record in this database describes one component's role in that architecture; this overview record describes how they connect, what flows between them, which contracts they share, how the whole would be tested, and what is genuinely built versus merely designed.

How the components connect. The user goal enters through program 100, the ecosystem, which hands it to program 1, the orchestrator, as the single point of planning. The orchestrator decomposes the goal and issues orders: build orders to the software factory (13), database orders to the constructor (21), generator orders to the foundry (23), and research questions to the cross-database research engine (27). The foundry (23) feeds the constructor (21): generators built by the foundry populate the databases the constructor creates, and the constructor's databases feed the research engine (27), which answers from real archived records rather than from claims. Everything that must run runs on the distributed execution fabric (56): factory builds, constructor loads, foundry generation, and research queries all execute there, so placement, failure, and recovery are handled once, uniformly. Nothing ships unverified: factory binaries go to the binary verification engine (52), which checks the actual binary, and computational results go to the replication engine (47), which re-runs them from recorded inputs and reports exactly what reproduced. The coverage auditor (78) closes the loop: it measures the archives the constructor and foundry produced, names the gaps, and reports them to the orchestrator (1), which plans the next round. The ecosystem (100) holds the shared contracts that make all of this compose: identity, version, dependency map, validation record, and recoverable source for every component.

Data flow, end to end. A goal arrives as a typed request with constraints, budget, and acceptance tests. The orchestrator turns it into a dependency graph of orders. Orders become artifacts: binaries from the factory, databases from the constructor, generators from the foundry, answers from the research engine. Every artifact carries identity, version, dependency map, validation record, and content hash. Verification results and replication reports flow back to the orchestrator alongside coverage-gap reports, and the orchestrator's next plan is built from those three feedback streams, never from optimism.

Shared contracts. Every component in the architecture honors the same common contract as every apex program: typed input, dependency-graph plan, real execution, independent verification, a real artifact, provenance, stable persistence, and benchmark-driven improvement with rollback. On top of that, the integrated architecture adds three shared rules of its own: every component's output must be addressable by stable identity; every inter-component message must carry its provenance; and no component may silently drop a failure, a gap, or a verification miss, it must report it upstream to the orchestrator.

Test plan (designed, not yet executed at full-system scale). Contract validation on every component interface; dependency-graph checks that reject cycles and missing inputs before execution; factory test suites that must pass before any binary ships; binary verification on shipped binaries; replication re-runs of every computational result with mismatches reported, not hidden; coverage audits after every construction round with named gaps; failure-injection drills on the execution fabric; and rollback drills proving a bad version can be replaced by the last verified one. Each test has a pass condition written before it runs.

What is genuinely built versus designed, stated plainly. Genuinely built: this database itself, its records, and the small demo programs in it, which validate the architecture's flow-graph logic and each component's contract logic. Designed, not built: all ten component systems themselves. No component in this architecture is claimed to exist as a working system, and no test in the test plan above is claimed to have been run at full-system scale. When a component is genuinely built and passes independent tests, its record will say so with evidence; until then, “designed” is the honest label for the whole architecture.

title: Universal Intelligence Orchestrator in the Integrated Architecture (Apex Program 1): Signature Edition
body:
Signature edition component record: Universal Intelligence Orchestrator as it functions inside the integrated apex architecture, labeled Signature throughout.

Receives the user goal, decomposes it, and sequences the whole architecture. It is the only component that talks to the user about the goal, and the only one authorized to re-plan when a stage reports failure or a budget breach.

Role in the integrated architecture: orchestrator. This component is program 1 of the apex set, and one of the ten programs in the starting combination (1, 13, 21, 23, 27, 47, 52, 56, 78, 100) that together form the single tested architecture described in the overview record.

Inputs it receives: typed orders or questions from the orchestrator (program 1) or from upstream components, each carrying constraints, budget, and acceptance tests, plus the artifacts and reports of the components that feed it, all with provenance attached.

Outputs it owes: a real artifact, verified by independent tests, carrying identity, version, dependency map, validation record, and content hash, plus a report of anything that failed, was missing, or could not be verified, sent upstream rather than hidden.

Shared contracts it honors: the common apex contract, input, plan, execution, verification, artifact, provenance, persistence, improvement, plus the architecture's three shared rules: stable identity for every output, provenance on every message, and no silent failures.

Speculative status, stated plainly: this component is a DESIGN CONCEPT within a designed architecture. Implementation status is “designed”. The demo below validates contract and flow-graph logic only; it does not claim this component system exists or works.
